title: How should Futhark expose irregular arrays to the programmer?
excerpt: A high-performance and high-level purely functional data-parallel array programming language that can execute on the GPU and CPU.
content_html:
Posted on August 12, 2026

Recently Futhark has grown some powerful new features such as flattening nonuniform data parallelism and recursive functions. While the latter is obviously user-visible, and we’ll see some nice uses later in this post, flattening is mainly a program transformation. Briefly, it lets the compiler handle expressions such as

map (\n -> i64.sum (iota n)) ns

where the size of the inner parallelism (n) differs between iterations of the outer map, and fully exploit all parallelism. Adding this did not fundamentally change which Futhark programs could be written, or their semantics, it merely had an effect on how good GPU code we could generate (and in extreme cases, whether we could generate GPU code at all). In this post we will see how the language can be extended to be fundamentally more expressive via a somewhat small extension, and what kinds of programs we can now write in Futhark.

Irregular arrays

The main language restriction in Futhark is that irregular arrays are not allowed. An irregular array is a multidimensional array where subarrays differ in size. For example, `[[1], [3,3]] is irregular, while [[1,2],[3,4]] is regular. The reason for this restriction is ultimately rooted in concerns for the efficiency of compilation, but the user experience is that these arrays are simply not well-typed in Futhark’s size type system. However, the main challenge in implementing flattening is handling the irregular arrays that arise as intermediate results when performing loop distribution:

map (\n -> i64.sum (iota n)) ns

↓

let tmps = map (\n -> iota n) ns
let res  = map (\tmp -> i64.sum tmp) tmps

This means that the flattening transformation is actually perfectly able to handle irregular arrays by encoding them as regular arrays, without the rest of the compiler having to know about it. Irregular arrays are definitely useful in some cases, so the question is how we can expose some of this power in the source language without adding general support for irregular arrays. As an example of the kind of code we would like to write, here is a recursive data-parallel quicksort written in NESL:

function quicksort(a) =
  if (#a < 2) then a
  else
    let pivot   = a[#a/2];
        lesser  = {e in a| e < pivot};
        equal   = {e in a| e == pivot};
        greater = {e in a| e > pivot};
        result  = {quicksort(v): v in [lesser,greater]};
    in result[0] ++ equal ++ result[1];

Note the main trick: mapping over a two-element array that performs the recursive quicksort calls, although in NESL this is done with an array comprehension rather than a map function. This array is irregular in NESL, which of course won’t fly in Futhark.

This will serve as our motivating example for a start, although we’ll see that quicksort is actually one of the simpler cases.

An initial flatmap SOAC

Futhark allows parallel programming via second-order array combinators (SOACs): functions such as map, reduce, and scan. We extend this with a new SOAC flatmap, that semantically is like map, except the results returned by the mapped function may differ in size, and flatmap returns the concatenation of the arrays:

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b : (f: (k: i64) -> (x: a) -> [k]b)
                     -> [n]i64
                     -> [n]a
                     -> ?[m].[m]b

Note the careful use of size types: flatmap accepts two arrays both of size n, and the first array (of type [n]i64) contains the expected sizes returned by the f function on the corresponding array of as. The size k is also passed to the mapped function so we can use it in its return type. The result of flatmap has existential size m, because we cannot know it in advance. (Actually, we can: m is the sum of the [n]i64 array.)

This is similar to Haskell’s concatMap, although the intention is that flatmap exploits parallelism across the n input elements and whatever parallelism may be in f. However, semantically flatmap is nothing special, and can easily be implemented with a sequential loop. Even the parallel implementation of flatmap (both this version and the ones below) is largely straightforward, as it is just a call to the “lifted” form of the provided function, so in this post we focus on whether flatmap provides the flexibility we need in order to express the algorithms we care about.

This flatmap is sufficient to implement a recursive quicksort in Futhark:

def quicksort [n] (xs: [n]i32) : [n]i32 =
  if n <= 1
  then xs
  else let pivot = xs[0]
       let [m][k] (lesser: [m]i32, greater: [k]i32) =
         partition (<= pivot) (drop 1 xs)
       let sorted =
         flatmap (\k p -> quicksort (sized k (if p then lesser else greater)))
                 [m, k]
                 [true, false]
       in sized n (take m sorted ++ [pivot] ++ drop m sorted)

The code looks slightly odder than a normal recursive quicksort. The oddity is constructing a two-element array just to flatmap it immediately rather than performing two recursive calls, but this is necessary in order to run the two recursive calls in parallel. In NESL this array is irregular, while in Futhark we construct an array of booleans ([true, false]) and use a conditional inside the flatmap function to pick either the lesser or greater array. I expect this may become a common trick when writing divide-and-conquer programs in Futhark.

Generalising flatmap

Although sufficient to express quicksort, the flatmap above has the restriction that we must be able to determine the size of each result in advance. This is sufficient for sorting, because sorting an array does not change its size, but is not practical for algorithms such as Quickhull, where the size of the result is usually smaller than the size of the input. The obvious extension is to modify flatmap such that the size of the array returned by the mapped function is existentially quantified:

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b : (f: (x: a) -> ?[k].[k]b)
                     -> [n]a
                     -> ?[m].[m]b

Now k is no longer a parameter to the f function, but bound in its return type. This means no longer know anything about the size of the result, which quickly turns out to be impractical. We therefore extend flatmap to also return the size of each array returned by f, in the form of a shape vector:

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b : (f: (x: a) -> ?[k].[k]b)
                     -> [n]a
                     -> ?[m].([n]i64, [m]b)

In fact, the real flatmap in the Futhark prelude returns not just the shape vector, but also various other related metadata that flattening computes anyway, but for simplicity we’ll stick with just the shape vector for this post.

Using this definition, we can implement Quickhull. I will not give the full program as it involves many functions for geometry calculations, but the recursive part can be written like this:

def hull [n] (a: point) (b: point) (pts: [n]point) : []point =
  if n <= 1
  then pts
  else let p = farthest a b pts
       let f i =
         let (x, y, pts') =
           if i == 0
           then (a, p, filter (\q -> side a p q > 0) pts)
           else (p, b, filter (\q -> side p b q > 0) pts)
         in hull x y pts'
       let (shape, pts') = flatmap f [0, 1]
       in take shape[0] pts' ++ [p] ++ take shape[1] pts'

We can actually write this in a slightly cleverer way that does not use shape at all - see the link if you are interested.

Generalising flatmap further

As a final generalisation, although one that we don’t yet have a concrete use case for, we also allow flatmap to return a uniform result for each input element, like a normal map. This gives us this final type:

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b 'c : (f: (x: a) -> ?[k].([k]b, c))
                        -> [n]a
                        -> ?[m].([n]i64, [m]b, [n]c)

Whenever we are not interested in a uniform result, we can simply instantiate c with (), and the prelude contains a wrapper named flatmap' that does this.

Although size types are by now a rather mature feature in Futhark, I do still get a pleasant surprise whenever they allow us to express the type of a function like flatmap in such a clear and precise manner.

With this generalisation, flatmap has now reached its final form. I like that it is such a small extension, barely even a “language extension” at all (although the compiler IR had to be modified), and that its semantics are completely trivial. The question is to what extent it is sufficient to express, say, NESL’s library of parallel algorithms in a clean manner, despite the language itself not supporting irregular arrays.

Performance

There’s a final wrinkle to the story: how fast is flatmap? In the flattening post I mentioned that performance of the nonuniform case had not yet been prioritised, and in the recursion post I mentioned that it seemed like recursion in a data parallel language could easily be very costly. We are now combining two inefficient things, so it is likely the spirit of the hedgehog may be somewhat lacking. But just how bad is it? We are in the fortunate situation that flatmap does not fundamentally increase the expressivity of the language, as it was always possible (if tedious and error-prone) to flatten by hand, so we do have hand-flattened versions of the algorithms we can now implement with recursive divide-and-conquer. For example, let us compare the quicksort from the https://github.com/diku-dk/sorts package with the recursive quicksort above:

-- ==
-- entry: bench_flatmap bench_manual
-- random input { [100000]i32 }

entry bench_flatmap = quicksort -- from above

module M = import "lib/github.com/diku-dk/sorts/quick_sort"

entry bench_manual = M.qsort (i32.<=)

Be aware that the qsort from the package is known to be fairly inefficient (we usually recommend merge- or radix-sort on GPUs), so none of the sorts here are even remotely fast in absolute terms. But let’s see how bad it is:

$ futhark bench --backend=cuda sortbench.fut
Compiling sortbench.fut...
Reporting arithmetic mean runtime of at least 10 runs for each dataset (min 0.5s).
More runs automatically performed for up to 300s to ensure accurate measurement.

sortbench.fut:bench_flatmap (no tuning file):
[100000]i32:     231986μs (95% CI: [  230655.0,   233282.1])

sortbench.fut:bench_manual (no tuning file):
[100000]i32:      12079μs (95% CI: [   12059.0,    12098.0])

Pretty awful stuff. I have not investigated just why bench_flatmap is so slow, but I suspect it is because of flattening producing a huge number of small kernels, as well as the intrinsic overhead of recursive calls, where each activation record maintains many large-ish arrays of flattening metadata and values. The hand-flattened quicksort (bench_manual) is very slow as sorts go because of the excessive bookkeeping, but it is written with a tail-recursive loop, and a minimal number of parallel operations.

It raises an interesting research question: can we automatically compile such recursive divide-and-conquer functions to something that is equivalent to manually flattened tail-recursive code? Yes, I remember writing about why I dislike tail call optimisation, but in this case it seems necessary to obtain good performance. This, however, is for the future, and if the program analysis becomes too tricky or fragile, we may need a dedicated SOAC for expressing various divide-and-conquer patterns in a way the compiler can exploit.

sentences.en: Futhark allows parallel programming via second-order array combinators (SOACs): functions such as map, reduce, and scan.
sentences.zh: Futhark 允许通过二阶数组组合器 (SOAC) 进行并行编程：map、reduce 和 scan 等函数。

sentences.en: We extend this with a new SOAC flatmap, that semantically is like map, except the results returned by the mapped function may differ in size, and flatmap returns the concatenation of the arrays:
sentences.zh: 我们用一个新的 SOAC 平面映射来扩展它，它在语义上类似于映射，除了映射函数返回的结果可能在大小上不同，并且平面映射返回数组的串联：

blocks.html_en: Note the careful use of size types: flatmap accepts two arrays both of size n, and the first array (of type [n]i64) contains the expected sizes returned by the f function on the corresponding array of as. The size k is also passed to the mapped function so we can use it in its return type. The result of flatmap has existential size m, because we cannot know it in advance. (Actually, we can: m is the sum of the [n]i64 array.)

sentences.en: Note the careful use of size types: flatmap accepts two arrays both of size n, and the first array (of type [n]i64) contains the expected sizes returned by the f function on the corresponding array of as.

sentences.zh: 大小 k 也传递给映射函数，因此我们可以在其返回类型中使用它。

sentences.zh: flatmap 的结果具有存在大小 m，因为我们无法提前知道它。

blocks.html_en: This is similar to Haskell’s concatMap, although the intention is that flatmap exploits parallelism across the n input elements and whatever parallelism may be in f. However, semantically flatmap is nothing special, and can easily be implemented with a sequential loop. Even the parallel implementation of flatmap (both this version and the ones below) is largely straightforward, as it is just a call to the “lifted” form of the provided function, so in this post we focus on whether flatmap provides the flexibility we need in order to express the algorithms we care about.

blocks.html_en: There’s a final wrinkle to the story: how fast is flatmap? In the flattening post I mentioned that performance of the nonuniform case had not yet been prioritised, and in the recursion post I mentioned that it seemed like recursion in a data parallel language could easily be very costly. We are now combining two inefficient things, so it is likely the spirit of the hedgehog may be somewhat lacking. But just how bad is it? We are in the fortunate situation that flatmap does not fundamentally increase the expressivity of the language, as it was always possible (if tedious and error-prone) to flatten by hand, so we do have hand-flattened versions of the algorithms we can now implement with recursive divide-and-conquer. content_html_zh:
发表于 2026 年 8 月 12 日

最近，Futhark 增加了一些强大的新功能，例如扁平化非均匀数据并行性和递归函数。 虽然后者显然是用户可见的，并且我们将在本文后面看到一些很好的用途，但扁平化主要是一种程序转换。 简而言之，它让编译器处理诸如

map (\n -> i64.sum (iota n)) ns

其中内部并行度 (n) 的大小在外部映射的迭代之间不同，并充分利用所有并行度。 添加这一点并没有从根本上改变可以编写的 Futhark 程序或其语义，它只会影响我们可以生成多好的 GPU 代码（在极端情况下，我们是否可以生成 GPU 代码）。 在这篇文章中，我们将看到如何通过一个较小的扩展来扩展该语言，从根本上更具表现力，以及我们现在可以用 Futhark 编写哪些类型的程序。

不规则阵列

Futhark 的主要语言限制是不允许使用不规则数组。 不规则数组是多维数组，其中子数组的大小不同。 例如，`[[1], [3,3]] 是不规则的，而 [[1,2],[3,4]] 是规则的。 这种限制的原因最终是出于对编译效率的考虑，但用户体验是这些数组在 Futhark 的大小类型系统中根本没有很好的类型。 然而，实现扁平化的主要挑战是处理执行循环分布时作为中间结果出现的不规则数组：

map (\n -> i64.sum (iota n)) ns

↓

let tmps = map (\n -> iota n) ns
let res  = map (\tmp -> i64.sum tmp) tmps

这意味着展平变换实际上能够通过将不规则数组编码为常规数组来完美地处理不规则数组，而编译器的其余部分不必知道这一点。 不规则数组在某些情况下肯定很有用，因此问题是我们如何在源语言中展示这种功能，而不添加对不规则数组的一般支持。 作为我们想要编写的代码类型的示例，以下是用 NESL 编写的递归数据并行快速排序：

function quicksort(a) =
  if (#a < 2) then a
  else
    let pivot   = a[#a/2];
        lesser  = {e in a| e < pivot};
        equal   = {e in a| e == pivot};
        greater = {e in a| e > pivot};
        result  = {quicksort(v): v in [lesser,greater]};
    in result[0] ++ equal ++ result[1];

请注意主要技巧：映射执行递归快速排序调用的二元素数组，尽管在 NESL 中这是通过数组理解而不是映射函数来完成的。 这个数组在 NESL 中是不规则的，当然在 Futhark 中是不会飞的。

这将作为我们开始的激励示例，尽管我们会看到快速排序实际上是更简单的情况之一。

初始平面 SOAC

Futhark 允许通过二阶数组组合器 (SOAC) 进行并行编程：map、reduce 和 scan 等函数。 我们用一个新的 SOAC 平面映射来扩展它，它在语义上类似于映射，除了映射函数返回的结果可能在大小上不同，并且平面映射返回数组的串联：

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b : (f: (k: i64) -> (x: a) -> [k]b)
                     -> [n]i64
                     -> [n]a
                     -> ?[m].[m]b

请注意大小类型的谨慎使用：flatmap 接受两个大小均为 n 的数组，第一个数组（类型为 [n]i64）包含 f 函数在 as 的相应数组上返回的预期大小。 大小 k 也传递给映射函数，因此我们可以在其返回类型中使用它。 flatmap 的结果具有存在大小 m，因为我们无法提前知道它。 （实际上，我们可以：m是[n]i64数组的和。）

这类似于 Haskell 的 concatMap，尽管其意图是 flatmap 利用 n 个输入元素的并行性以及 f 中可能存在的任何并行性。 然而，语义上的平面图并没有什么特别的，并且可以很容易地通过顺序循环来实现。 即使是 flatmap 的并行实现（无论是这个版本还是下面的版本）也很简单，因为它只是对所提供函数的“提升”形式的调用，因此在这篇文章中，我们重点关注 flatmap 是否提供了我们需要的灵活性来表达我们关心的算法。

这个平面图足以在 Futhark 中实现递归快速排序：

def quicksort [n] (xs: [n]i32) : [n]i32 =
  if n <= 1
  then xs
  else let pivot = xs[0]
       let [m][k] (lesser: [m]i32, greater: [k]i32) =
         partition (<= pivot) (drop 1 xs)
       let sorted =
         flatmap (\k p -> quicksort (sized k (if p then lesser else greater)))
                 [m, k]
                 [true, false]
       in sized n (take m sorted ++ [pivot] ++ drop m sorted)

该代码看起来比普通的递归快速排序稍微奇怪。 奇怪的是构造一个二元素数组只是为了立即对其进行平面映射，而不是执行两个递归调用，但为了并行运行两个递归调用，这是必要的。 在 NESL 中，这个数组是不规则的，而在 Futhark 中，我们构造一个布尔数组 ([true, false])，并在 flatmap 函数中使用条件来选择较小或较大的数组。 我预计这可能会成为在 Futhark 中编写分而治之程序时的常见技巧。

概括平面图

尽管足以表达快速排序，但上面的平面图有一个限制，即我们必须能够提前确定每个结果的大小。 这对于排序来说已经足够了，因为对数组进行排序不会改变其大小，但对于像 Quickhull 这样的算法来说并不实用，因为在这种算法中，结果的大小通常小于输入的大小。 明显的扩展是修改 flatmap，使得映射函数返回的数组的大小是存在量化的：

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b : (f: (x: a) -> ?[k].[k]b)
                     -> [n]a
                     -> ?[m].[m]b

现在 k 不再是 f 函数的参数，而是绑定在其返回类型中。 这意味着不再知道结果的大小，这很快就被证明是不切实际的。 因此，我们扩展 flatmap 来以形状向量的形式返回 f 返回的每个数组的大小：

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b : (f: (x: a) -> ?[k].[k]b)
                     -> [n]a
                     -> ?[m].([n]i64, [m]b)

事实上，Futhark prelude 中的真实平面图不仅返回形状向量，还返回扁平化计算的各种其他相关元数据，但为了简单起见，我们将在本文中仅使用形状向量。

使用这个定义，我们可以实现 Quickhull。 我不会给出完整的程序，因为它涉及许多几何计算的函数，但递归部分可以这样写：

def hull [n] (a: point) (b: point) (pts: [n]point) : []point =
  if n <= 1
  then pts
  else let p = farthest a b pts
       let f i =
         let (x, y, pts') =
           if i == 0
           then (a, p, filter (\q -> side a p q > 0) pts)
           else (p, b, filter (\q -> side p b q > 0) pts)
         in hull x y pts'
       let (shape, pts') = flatmap f [0, 1]
       in take shape[0] pts' ++ [p] ++ take shape[1] pts'

实际上，我们可以用一种稍微聪明的方式来编写它，根本不使用形状 - 如果您感兴趣，请参阅链接。

进一步概括平面图

作为最后的概括，虽然我们还没有具体的用例，但我们也允许平面地图为每个输入元素返回统一的结果，就像法线贴图一样。 这给了我们最终的类型：

val flatmap [n] 'a 'b 'c : (f: (x: a) -> ?[k].([k]b, c))
                        -> [n]a
                        -> ?[m].([n]i64, [m]b, [n]c)

每当我们对统一结果不感兴趣时​​，我们可以简单地用 () 实例化 c，并且 prelude 包含一个名为 flatmap' 的包装器来执行此操作。

尽管尺寸类型现在已经是 Futhark 中相当成熟的功能，但每当它们允许我们以如此清晰和精确的方式表达像 flatmap 这样的函数类型时，我仍然会感到惊喜。

通过这种概括，平面地图现已达到其最终形式。 我喜欢它这么小的扩展，甚至根本不是一个“语言扩展”（尽管必须修改编译器 IR），而且它的语义完全微不足道。 问题是，尽管语言本身不支持不规则数组，但在多大程度上足以以干净的方式表达例如 NESL 的并行算法库。

表现

这个故事还有最后一个问题：平面地图有多快？ 在扁平化帖子中，我提到非均匀情况的性能尚未得到优先考虑，并且在递归帖子中我提到，数据并行语言中的递归似乎很容易变得非常昂贵。 我们现在将两种低效的东西结合在一起，所以刺猬的精神可能会有所欠缺。 但到底有多糟糕呢？ 幸运的是，平面映射并没有从根本上提高语言的表达能力，因为总是可以（如果乏味且容易出错）手动展平，因此我们确实有算法的手动展平版本，现在可以通过递归分而治之来实现。 例如，让我们将 https://github.com/diku-dk/sorts 包中的快速排序与上面的递归快速排序进行比较：

-- ==
-- entry: bench_flatmap bench_manual
-- random input { [100000]i32 }

entry bench_flatmap = quicksort -- from above

module M = import "lib/github.com/diku-dk/sorts/quick_sort"

entry bench_manual = M.qsort (i32.<=)

请注意，众所周知，该包中的 qsort 效率相当低（我们通常建议在 GPU 上进行合并排序或基数排序），因此这里的排序从绝对值来看都远非快。 但让我们看看情况有多糟糕：

$ futhark bench --backend=cuda sortbench.fut
Compiling sortbench.fut...
Reporting arithmetic mean runtime of at least 10 runs for each dataset (min 0.5s).
More runs automatically performed for up to 300s to ensure accurate measurement.

sortbench.fut:bench_flatmap (no tuning file):
[100000]i32:     231986μs (95% CI: [  230655.0,   233282.1])

sortbench.fut:bench_manual (no tuning file):
[100000]i32:      12079μs (95% CI: [   12059.0,    12098.0])

非常糟糕的东西。 我还没有调查为什么 bench_flatmap 如此慢，但我怀疑这是因为展平产生了大量的小内核，以及递归调用的固有开销，其中每个激活记录维护许多大型的展平元数据​​和值数组。 由于过多的簿记，手工扁平快速排序（bench_manual）在排序过程中非常慢，但它是用尾递归循环和最少数量的并行操作编写的。

它提出了一个有趣的研究问题：我们能否自动将这种递归分治函数编译为相当于手动扁平尾递归代码的东西？ 是的，我记得写过为什么我不喜欢尾调用优化，但在这种情况下，似乎有必要获得良好的性能。 然而，这是面向未来的，如果程序分析变得过于棘手或脆弱，我们可能需要一个专用的 SOAC 来以编译器可以利用的方式表达各种分而治之的模式。
